## Hard-to-vary test: Anselm's *Proslogion*, with Gaunilo's reply

**1. The question, frozen.** The document answers several questions. The one its title and opening make central is Chapter 2's: does "something greater than which cannot be thought" exist in reality, and not only in thought? Range: any being so described, for any hearer, fool or believer. Asked: which existence does it have? I hold it there. The material on *Cur Deus Homo* in the introduction (why God had to become man) is a second question — about God's motives, not his existence — and I leave it out. Gaunilo's reply is a rival inside the same document, not a new question.

**2. The parts**, in Anselm's words. P1 "something greater than which cannot be thought". P2 "he understands what he heard". P3 "whatever is understood exists in thought". P4 the painter: "it is one thing for something to exist in a person's thought and quite another for the person to think that thing exists". P5 "if it exists only in thought it could also be thought of as existing in reality as well, which is greater". P6 (Ch. 3) "it cannot be thought of as not existing". P7 (Ch. 4) a thing "is thought in one way when the words signifying it are thought", and "in quite another way when the thing signified is understood".

Jobs. **J1** why it exists in reality and not only in thought (*given*). **J2** why the fool could say "there is no God" (*given* — Anselm raises it himself). **J3** why it cannot be thought not to exist (*given*, Ch. 3). **J4** why it is not Gaunilo's lost island (*given*, by Gaunilo). **J5** something we could check that would differ if it existed in thought only (*added* by me — so any part held only by J5 is *held if* J5 is real, which at present it is not).

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **Held if** | Removing it stops J1 dead. But swap the subject for Gaunilo's "island… superior in the abundance of its riches to all other lands" and the identical steps run. What both share is *an unsurpassable thing*, so that, not the word "greater", is the part doing the work. Anselm's reply separates God from the island only by leaning on P6, which is itself in doubt. |
| P2 | **Held** | J2 needs the fool to have understood what he heard. |
| P3 | **Held** — but it is a reading | It moves when the hearer's words change, and stays put when nothing about God changes. It measures the thinker, not the thing. |
| P4 | **Held** | It separates two senses of "in the mind", and Gaunilo grants the distinction even while denying it carries the move. |
| P5 | **Borrowed** | Rests on a ranking — existing in reality outranks existing in thought — that is never argued and that Gaunilo denies outright. |
| P6 | **Held if** | Carries J3 only. It is a fact about thinkers dressed as a property of God (see reverse, below). |
| P7 | **Held if** | Carries J2 alone, and rescues it by narrowing: "no one who understands what God is can think that he does not exist". |
| "sin has so darkened our minds" / the fool is "stupid and foolish" | **Borrowed, acting as a catch-all** | Ch. 1's premise. Any failure to see the proof is charged to sin or stupidity; no gauge is offered — nothing would count as the argument, rather than the mind, being at fault. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**

*Flip the outcome.* Give the being existence in thought only. The same steps still reach reality, because P5 does the work whatever the case. Run the same steps on the island and they reach the island. An argument that returns its conclusion whatever the world is like is held in place by nothing in the world.

*Hunt the answer in the starting points.* Anselm's reply says the being "cannot be thought of except as having no beginning" — eternity sitting among the starting points. Gaunilo says it plainly: "It should first be proved conclusively that some being superior… exists, so that on this basis we can go on to prove the attributes such a greater and better being must possess."

*Direction.* Ch. 3 runs from a fact about thinkers ("cannot be thought of as not existing") to a claim about God. Anselm himself, in Ch. 1, cannot find God anywhere: "I have never seen you… or known your face." Gaunilo's poke lands exactly here: "I am absolutely certain that I exist, although I nevertheless know that my nonexistence is possible"; and if he cannot think himself away, "the impossibility of doing so will not be something peculiar to thinking about God."

*The change list.* It contains no change to the world — nothing to point at, sail to, or measure. The one member on the list that could have been checked is Gaunilo's island, and Anselm leaves it by a distinction that presupposes P6.

*Patches.* Ch. 4 is a patch made after the fool's denial appeared. It buys the rescue by narrowing the claim, and the added part (two ways of thinking) has no other job.

*Rival and provenance.* Gaunilo's "bare words, and… an affection produced by the words within his soul" is a properly built rival, and no change on the list separates it from Anselm's. Anselm does keep fair records: he states he is changing the claim ("Never in my entire treatise do I say this") and concedes at the end that "it is not… so easy to prove the same thing of 'that which is greater than all other things'." P1, P3, P5 are *asserted*; P7 is *fitted* to the fool case; Ch. 1's frame is *borrowed* from revelation, which Anselm says openly. This part, unlike the rest of the document, is honest bookkeeping.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Two things. (a) One pokeable difference: something a person could check that comes out one way if the being exists in reality and another if it exists in thought alone. (b) A demonstration that the argument fails on the island without already assuming P6. Anselm's last sentence points at (b).

**6. What this does not show.** Failing does not show God does not exist; passing would not have shown he does. This tests the argument's grip, not the truth. Nothing here is poked in the physical sense: the changes are changes to conditions and to the speaker, and comparisons here hold parts far less tightly than a laboratory does.

**7. One next step.** Run the island argument with the necessity clause added — "an island than which a greater cannot be thought, and which cannot be thought not to exist" — and see whether anything but the words stops it.
